title: The warn ring is src/fx/warn-ring.js; the wave clock stays in the frame for a later round
context: The refactor run's Task 13 planned two moves: the warn rings (the pooled point cloud every warning ring is drawn in) to an fx module, and the frame's wave clock to a pure domain rule that returns its decisions for the controller to perform.
outcome: src/fx/warn-ring.js (createWarnRing(scene, host): ring, tick) owns the cloud, its buffers and the rings; td-tab keeps warnRing and stepWarnFx as one-liners for its thirteen callers. The wave clock did NOT move: its seven lets (wave, waveActive, waveAge, waveIn, waveCharge, warnBeat, interClock) are read and written at about twenty controller sites (the enemy step's setters, the HUD chip, the boss omen, the acceptance hooks), and the cleared branch interleaves the clock's writes with the score, the sim curve, the sector's hold and the sitrep, so returning decisions would reorder effects. A faithful move needs those lets gathered into one state object first; that is the next round's first step. A side effect of the import line growing: td-tab line 63 passed 500 characters and the guard caught it; the line is split in two (no token change).
alternatives: Move the clock now behind getters and setters for the seven lets: rejected, it would be the 44-member host problem again in miniature, and the decisions interface the plan sketched would reorder side effects.
evidence: Equivalence harness (session scratchpad warn-equiv.mjs): three rings started, aged and drawn over 50 frames: the original block and the module write identical buffers; test/warn-ring.mjs pins the digest
undef-diff and host contracts (44 factories) clean; npm run check caught and then passed the long import line
